- Manusmṛti
- Mahābhārata (Śāntiparva)
- Arthaśāstra (Kauṭilya)
- Dharmasūtras (Āpastamba, Gautama)

# Karma

## Canonical Name

Karma

## Sanskrit

कर्म

## Transliteration

Karma

## Śabda

कर्म

## Dhātu

कृ (Kṛ) — To do, perform, act, make.

## Vyākaraṇa

Derived from the verbal root कृ (kṛ) with the suffix -man (neuter noun). Pāṇini Ashtadhyayi 3.3.18. Karma is a neuter noun meaning "action" or "deed." In grammar, karma also denotes the object of a verb (karman = object/patient).

## Nirukta

Yāska: "kriyate anena iti karma" — that by which action is performed. The root kṛ encompasses all forms of doing, making, and performing.

## Bīja

क (Ka) — the seed syllable of action and creation in Tantric traditions. Associated with Brahmā (the creator) whose bīja is also Ka.

## Tattva

Karma-Tattva — the principle of causation through action. In Sāṃkhya: karma is the activity of the three guṇas (sattva, rajas, tamas). In Vaiśeṣika: karma is one of the seven padārthas (categories), defined as motion. In Vedānta: karma is the mechanism of saṃsāra (cycle of rebirth).

## Śakti

Kriyā-Śakti — the power of action. One of the three fundamental śaktis (icchā-jñāna-kriyā). Karma operates through kriyā-śakti as the dynamic force of manifestation.

## Literal Meaning

Action; deed; work; ritual act.

## Functional Meaning

Karma is the universal principle that every action generates corresponding consequences. It operates across three dimensions: Sañcita karma (accumulated past actions), Prārabdha karma (karma currently bearing fruit), and Āgāmi/Kriyamāṇa karma (karma being created now). The law of karma is not punishment but the natural law of cause and effect operating through consciousness.

## Ontology

In Mīmāṃsā: karma (ritual action) is the primary means of achieving dharmic results; the apūrva (unseen potency) of ritual karma persists until it bears fruit. In Advaita Vedānta: karma operates only at the vyāvahārika level; from the absolute standpoint, there is no doer, hence no karma. In Viśiṣṭādvaita: karma is real and must be exhausted through bhakti and surrender to Viṣṇu. In Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika: karma is one of seven categories of reality, defined as motion (pariṇāma).

## Cosmology

Karma drives the cycle of saṃsāra across all fourteen lokas. The Purāṇas describe karma as the mechanism by which souls transmigrate through different realms. In Jain cosmology, karma is a subtle material substance (karma-pudgala) that adheres to the soul (jīva) and determines its condition. The Bhāgavata Purāṇa describes karma as the force that maintains the cosmic order of creation, preservation, and dissolution.

## Psychology

In Yoga psychology: karma creates saṃskāras (mental impressions) and vāsanās (latent tendencies) that condition future experience. Patañjali's Yoga Sūtras 2.12-14 describe the karma-āśaya (karma-store) as the root of birth, lifespan, and experience. Karma operates through the kāraṇa-śarīra (causal body). Karma yoga (the yoga of action) transforms karma from bondage to liberation by eliminating the sense of doership (ahaṃkāra).

## Marathi Summary

कर्मयोग म्हणजे आपले कर्तव्यकर्म करणे, पण त्याच्या फळाची आसक्ती न ठेवणे. अशा कृतीतून अहंभाव कमी होतो आणि कर्मबंधनातून मुक्त होण्याचा मार्ग मिळतो.

## Governance

Karma as social principle: the concept of karma-phala (fruit of action) underlies Indian jurisprudence. Kauṭilya's Arthaśāstra recognizes that rulers accumulate karma through their governance. The concept of rāja-dharma (royal duty) is the karmic responsibility of the king. Historical Indian governance was explicitly framed in karmic terms — Aśoka's dhamma edicts reflect karmic accountability.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: karma is one of the causes of disease (prājñāparādha — crime against wisdom is a karmic cause). Caraka Saṃhitā identifies karma as a factor in the etiology of disease. Karmic diseases (ādhidaivika) require spiritual remedies alongside physical treatment. The concept of karma-ja-vyādhi (karma-born disease) is a distinct category in Āyurvedic pathology.

## Mathematics

The mathematical principle of karma is the law of conservation: every action has an equal and opposite reaction. Vedic mathematics (Gaṇita) treats karma as the principle of balance — equations must balance, debts must be settled. The concept of ṛṇa (debt) in Vedic mathematics mirrors the karmic debt concept.

## Astronomy

Karma in Jyotiṣa (Vedic astrology): the birth chart (janma-kuṇḍali) is considered a map of prārabdha karma. Planetary positions at birth reflect accumulated karma. The concept of daśā (planetary period) describes the timing of karmic fruition. Graha (planets) are considered agents of karma delivery.

## Metallurgy

In Viśvakarmā tradition: the karma of the craftsman (śilpin) determines the quality of the work. The concept of karma-yoga in craft: the craftsman who works without attachment to results produces the finest work. The dharma of metals (their inherent properties) must be respected — working against a metal's karma produces inferior results.

## Ritual

Karma-kāṇḍa (ritual section of the Vedas) is the primary domain of Mīmāṃsā. The sixteen saṃskāras are karmic rituals that shape the individual's karmic trajectory. Yajña (sacrifice) is the highest karmic act — it purifies accumulated karma and generates positive karma. Prāyaścitta (expiation) rituals neutralize specific karmic debts.

## Symbolism

The wheel (cakra) symbolizes karma's cyclical nature. The scales represent karmic balance. The seed (bīja) represents karma's potential — every action is a seed that will bear fruit. The mirror represents karma's reflective nature — what you do returns to you. The knot (granthi) represents karmic bondage.

## Related Deities

- Yama (Dharmarāja — lord of karmic accounting and death)
- Citragupta (Yama's scribe who records all karma)
- Śani (Saturn — the planet of karmic lessons and consequences)
- Brahmā (the creator who sets karma in motion)
- Viṣṇu (the preserver who maintains karmic order)

## Related Lokas

- Naraka (hell realms — destination of negative karma)
- Svarga (heaven realms — destination of positive karma)
- Pitṛloka (realm of ancestors — intermediate karmic state)
- Bhūloka (earth — the primary field of karmic action)

## Related Koshas

- Kāraṇa Śarīra (causal body) — the storehouse of accumulated karma (sañcita karma)
- Sūkṣma Śarīra (subtle body) — the vehicle through which karma is experienced
- Manomaya Kosha (mind sheath) — where karmic intentions originate

## Related Chakras

- Maṇipūra (solar plexus chakra) — seat of will, action, and karmic agency
- Mūlādhāra (root chakra) — seat of prārabdha karma and survival instincts
- Svādhiṣṭhāna (sacral chakra) — seat of karmic desires and creative action

## Related Yantras

- Karma Yantra (used in rituals for karmic purification)
- Śani Yantra (for mitigating difficult karmic periods)

## Related Mantras

- "Karmaṇy evādhikāras te mā phaleṣu kadācana" (Bhagavad Gītā 2.47) — You have the right to action alone, never to its fruits
- Mahāmṛtyuñjaya Mantra (for liberation from karmic death-cycle)
- Śani Mantra: "Om śam śanaiścarāya namaḥ" (for karmic lessons)

## Related Vidyās

- Karma-Yoga Vidyā (science of action without attachment)
- Jyotiṣa Vidyā (science of karmic timing)
- Prāyaścitta Vidyā (science of karmic expiation)

## Related Śāstras

- Bhagavad Gītā (Chapters 3, 4, 5 — Karma Yoga)
- Mīmāṃsā Sūtras (Jaimini) — ritual karma
- Yoga Sūtras (Patañjali) 2.12-14 — karma-āśaya
- Tattvartha Sūtra (Umāsvāti) — Jain karma doctrine
- Caraka Saṃhitā — karmic disease

## Traditional Interpretations

- Advaita Vedānta (Śaṅkara): Karma is ultimately unreal from the absolute standpoint; jñāna (knowledge) alone destroys karma
- Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja): Karma is real and must be surrendered to Viṣṇu through prapatti (surrender)
- Dvaita (Madhva): Karma is eternally real; liberation requires Viṣṇu's grace to transcend karma
- Mīmāṃsā: Karma (ritual action) is the primary means of achieving all human goals
- Buddhism: Karma is intentional action (cetanā); it is the intention, not the act, that creates karma
- Jainism: Karma is a subtle material substance that binds the soul; liberation requires exhausting all karma through tapas (austerity)

## Historical Evolution

- Ṛgvedic period: Karma primarily means ritual action; cosmic karma (ṛta) governs the universe
- Brāhmaṇa period: Karma as ritual action is elaborated extensively; karma-kāṇḍa develops
- Upaniṣadic period: Karma as ethical-spiritual principle emerges; karma-saṃsāra connection established
- Buddhist period (500 BCE): Karma redefined as intentional action; karma-rebirth doctrine systematized
- Jain period: Karma as material substance — unique and influential formulation
- Epic-Purāṇic period: Karma as cosmic justice mechanism; karma-yoga as path to liberation
- Medieval: Karma integrated into bhakti traditions — karma surrendered to God

## Cross References

- Dharma
- Moksha
- Yoga
- Saṃskāra
- Punarjanma (rebirth)
- Ahaṃkāra (ego — the false doer)
- Vāsanā (latent tendencies)

## Open Research Questions

- Is karma a deterministic or probabilistic system? Can free will operate within karma?
- What is the relationship between Vedic karma (ritual action) and Buddhist karma (intentional action)?
- How does the Jain material karma theory relate to the Vedic subtle-body karma theory?

## Experimental Hypotheses

[EXPERIMENTAL — NOT CANONICAL] Some researchers propose that karma theory anticipates modern concepts of information conservation in physics — that the "information" of every action is preserved in the universe. This remains speculative and is not established in any canonical tradition.

## Literal Meaning

That which is upheld; that which upholds. The sustaining principle.

## Functional Meaning

Dharma is the universal principle governing righteous conduct, cosmic order, social duty, and individual ethics. It operates simultaneously at four levels: Ṛta (cosmic order), Varṇāśrama-dharma (social order), Svadharma (individual duty), and Sādhāraṇa-dharma (universal ethics applicable to all beings).

धर्म म्हणजे योग्य आचरण, सामाजिक कर्तव्य, वैश्विक व्यवस्था आणि सर्वांसाठी लागू होणारी नैतिकता टिकवून ठेवणारे तत्त्व.

## Ontology

In Vaiśeṣika: Dharma is a padārtha (category of reality) — the cause of abhyudaya (worldly prosperity) and niḥśreyasa (liberation). In Mīmāṃsā: Dharma is codanā-lakṣaṇa — that which is enjoined by Vedic injunction. In Advaita Vedānta: Dharma at the vyāvahārika (conventional) level is real and necessary; at the pāramārthika (absolute) level, only Brahman exists.

## Cosmology

Dharma is one of the four Puruṣārthas (aims of human life): Dharma, Artha, Kāma, Mokṣa. In the Purāṇic cosmology, Dharma is personified as a deity, son of Brahmā, husband of ten daughters of Dakṣa. ## Psychology

In Yoga psychology (Patañjali): Dharma-megha-samādhi is the highest samādhi, the "cloud of virtue" that rains liberation. Dharma as psychological principle governs the sattva-rajas-tamas balance in the individual. Right action (dharmic action) produces psychological clarity (citta-prasāda).

## Governance

Rājadharma (royal duty) is elaborated in Manusmṛti, Arthaśāstra, Mahābhārata Śāntiparva. The king's primary duty is dharma-rakṣaṇa (protection of dharma). Ṛta (cosmic order, precursor to dharma) governs the movements of celestial bodies. Vedic astronomy (Jyotiṣa) treats planetary motion as dharmic — planets follow their ordained paths. The concept of ṛtu (season) derives from ṛta, linking dharma to astronomical cycles.

In Viśvakarmā tradition: the dharma of metals is their inherent nature and proper use. Gold (suvarṇa) has the dharma of purity; iron (ayasa) has the dharma of strength. Proper metallurgical practice follows the dharma of each material.

## Ritual

Yajña (sacrifice) is the primary ritual expression of dharma. The Mīmāṃsā school holds that Vedic ritual injunctions (vidhi) define dharma. Dharma-śāstra prescribes the sixteen saṃskāras (life-cycle rituals) as the ritual framework of dharmic life. Sandhyāvandana (daily worship) is the minimal dharmic ritual obligation.

## Symbolism

Dharma is symbolized by the wheel (dharmacakra) — the Buddha's first teaching is the "turning of the wheel of dharma." The scales of justice represent dharma's balancing function. The lotus represents dharma's purity amid worldly existence. The cow (go) is the living symbol of dharma in Vedic tradition.

- Yama (Dharmarāja — lord of dharma and death)
- Mitra (Vedic deity of contracts and dharmic agreements)
- Varuṇa (upholder of ṛta, cosmic dharma)
- Indra (protector of dharmic order against adharma)

- Satyaloka (Brahmaloka — realm of ultimate dharma)
- Pitṛloka (realm governed by ancestral dharma)

- Manomaya Kosha (mind sheath) — where dharmic intentions form
- Ānandamaya Kosha (bliss sheath) — the state of perfect dharmic alignment

## Related Chakras

- Anāhata (heart chakra) — seat of dharmic compassion and right relationship
- Ājñā (third eye chakra) — seat of dharmic wisdom and discrimination
- Sahasrāra (crown chakra) — union with cosmic dharma (Ṛta)

## Related Yantras

- Śrī Yantra (represents the cosmic order that dharma upholds)
- Dharma Yantra (specific to dharmic protection rituals)

## Related Mantras

- "Dharmo rakṣati rakṣitaḥ" (Manusmṛti 8.15) — Dharma protects those who protect it
- Gāyatrī Mantra (the foundational mantra of dharmic life)
- "Satyam vada, dharmam cara" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.11.1) — Speak truth, follow dharma

## Related Vidyās

- Dharmaśāstra Vidyā (science of righteous law)
- Rājadharma Vidyā (science of governance)
- Ātmavidyā (self-knowledge as the highest dharma)

## Related Śāstras

- Manusmṛti (primary dharmaśāstra)
- Yājñavalkya Smṛti
- Arthaśāstra (Kauṭilya)
- Mahābhārata (Śāntiparva, Anuśāsanaparva)
- Dharmasūtras of Āpastamba, Gautama, Baudhāyana

## Traditional Interpretations

- Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja): Dharma is bhakti-yoga — devotional service to Viṣṇu is the highest dharma
- Dvaita (Madhva): Dharma is the eternal will of Viṣṇu; individual dharma is participation in divine order
- Mīmāṃsā (Jaimini): Dharma is exclusively Vedic injunction; no dharma exists outside Veda
- Buddhism: Dharma is the teaching of the Buddha and the nature of reality (dhamma)
- Jainism: Dharma is the medium of motion (one of the six dravyas); also righteous conduct (dharma)

## Historical Evolution

- Ṛgvedic period: Ṛta (cosmic order) is the precursor; dharma appears rarely
- Atharvaveda: Dharma begins to acquire social and ethical dimensions
- Upaniṣadic period: Dharma becomes internalized as ethical-spiritual principle
- Epic period (Mahābhārata): Dharma becomes the central problematic — the Gītā's entire teaching is dharmic

## Canonical Name

Ahimsa

## Sanskrit

अहिंसा

## Transliteration

Ahimsa

Non-violence; non-harm; non-injury. From Sanskrit a (not) + himsa (violence, harm, injury).

## Ahimsa Paramo Dharma

The phrase **Ahimsa Paramo Dharma** (अहिंसा परमो धर्मः) means:

**"Non-violence is the highest dharma."**

- Ahimsa = non-violence
- Paramo = highest, supreme
- Dharma = duty, righteousness, cosmic order

## Functional Meaning

Ahimsa is the principle of not causing harm to any living being — in thought, word, or action. It is the foundational ethical principle shared across Hindu, Jain, and Buddhist traditions. In Jainism, ahimsa is the first and supreme vow. In Yoga, ahimsa is the first of the five Yamas (ethical restraints) in Patanjali's Ashtanga Yoga. In the Mahabharata, ahimsa is declared the highest dharma.

## Marathi Summary

अहिंसा म्हणजे विचार, शब्द किंवा कृतीतून कोणत्याही सजीवाला इजा न करणे. जैन परंपरेत ती सर्वोच्च व्रत मानली जाते.

The Acharanga Sutra (the oldest Jain canonical text) states the core teaching of ahimsa:

"All beings desire to live. None wishes to die. Therefore, a wise person does not kill, nor causes others to kill, nor consents to killing."

The Five Great Vows (Mahavrata) for Jain monks place Ahimsa first:
1. Ahimsa — Non-violence toward all living beings
2. Satya — Absolute truthfulness
3. Asteya — Non-stealing
4. Brahmacharya — Celibacy
5. Aparigraha — Complete non-possessiveness

UniGuru Citation: Acharanga Sutra, Book 1, Lecture 7; Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22, Jacobi translation

## Yoga Teaching on Ahimsa

In Patanjali's Yoga Sutras (2.30), Ahimsa is the first of the five Yamas:
"Ahimsa-satya-asteya-brahmacharya-aparigraha yamah" — Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the five restraints.

Patanjali states (Yoga Sutras 2.35): "Ahimsa-pratishthayam tat-sannidhau vaira-tyagah" — When one is established in non-violence, all enmity is abandoned in one's presence.

## Cosmology and Ethics

Ahimsa operates at multiple levels:
- Physical: not harming the body of any being
- Verbal: not speaking words that harm
- Mental: not harboring harmful thoughts

- Yoga (ahimsa is the first Yama in Patanjali's system)

- Acharanga Sutra (Jain canonical source — oldest text on ahimsa)
- Yoga Sutras of Patanjali (2.30 — ahimsa as first Yama)
- Caraka Samhita (Ayurvedic ethics — ahimsa as physician's duty)

# Karma

## Canonical Name

Karma

## Sanskrit

कर्म

## Transliteration

Karma

## Śabda

कर्म

## Dhātu

कृ (Kṛ) — To do, perform, act, make.

## Vyākaraṇa

Derived from the verbal root कृ (kṛ) with the suffix -man (neuter noun). Pāṇini Ashtadhyayi 3.3.18. Karma is a neuter noun meaning "action" or "deed." In grammar, karma also denotes the object of a verb (karman = object/patient).

## Nirukta

Yāska: "kriyate anena iti karma" — that by which action is performed. The root kṛ encompasses all forms of doing, making, and performing.

## Bīja

क (Ka) — the seed syllable of action and creation in Tantric traditions. Associated with Brahmā (the creator) whose bīja is also Ka.

## Tattva

Karma-Tattva — the principle of causation through action. In Sāṃkhya: karma is the activity of the three guṇas (sattva, rajas, tamas). In Vaiśeṣika: karma is one of the seven padārthas (categories), defined as motion. In Vedānta: karma is the mechanism of saṃsāra (cycle of rebirth).

## Śakti

Kriyā-Śakti — the power of action. One of the three fundamental śaktis (icchā-jñāna-kriyā). Karma operates through kriyā-śakti as the dynamic force of manifestation.

## Literal Meaning

Action; deed; work; ritual act.

## Functional Meaning

Karma is the universal principle that every action generates corresponding consequences. It operates across three dimensions: Sañcita karma (accumulated past actions), Prārabdha karma (karma currently bearing fruit), and Āgāmi/Kriyamāṇa karma (karma being created now). The law of karma is not punishment but the natural law of cause and effect operating through consciousness.

## Ontology

In Mīmāṃsā: karma (ritual action) is the primary means of achieving dharmic results; the apūrva (unseen potency) of ritual karma persists until it bears fruit. In Advaita Vedānta: karma operates only at the vyāvahārika level; from the absolute standpoint, there is no doer, hence no karma. In Viśiṣṭādvaita: karma is real and must be exhausted through bhakti and surrender to Viṣṇu. In Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika: karma is one of seven categories of reality, defined as motion (pariṇāma).

## Cosmology

Karma drives the cycle of saṃsāra across all fourteen lokas. The Purāṇas describe karma as the mechanism by which souls transmigrate through different realms. In Jain cosmology, karma is a subtle material substance (karma-pudgala) that adheres to the soul (jīva) and determines its condition. The Bhāgavata Purāṇa describes karma as the force that maintains the cosmic order of creation, preservation, and dissolution.

## Psychology

In Yoga psychology: karma creates saṃskāras (mental impressions) and vāsanās (latent tendencies) that condition future experience. Patañjali's Yoga Sūtras 2.12-14 describe the karma-āśaya (karma-store) as the root of birth, lifespan, and experience. Karma operates through the kāraṇa-śarīra (causal body). Karma yoga (the yoga of action) transforms karma from bondage to liberation by eliminating the sense of doership (ahaṃkāra).

## Marathi Summary

कर्मयोग म्हणजे आपले कर्तव्यकर्म करणे, पण त्याच्या फळाची आसक्ती न ठेवणे. अशा कृतीतून अहंभाव कमी होतो आणि कर्मबंधनातून मुक्त होण्याचा मार्ग मिळतो.

## Governance

Karma as social principle: the concept of karma-phala (fruit of action) underlies Indian jurisprudence. Kauṭilya's Arthaśāstra recognizes that rulers accumulate karma through their governance. The concept of rāja-dharma (royal duty) is the karmic responsibility of the king. Historical Indian governance was explicitly framed in karmic terms — Aśoka's dhamma edicts reflect karmic accountability.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: karma is one of the causes of disease (prājñāparādha — crime against wisdom is a karmic cause). Caraka Saṃhitā identifies karma as a factor in the etiology of disease. Karmic diseases (ādhidaivika) require spiritual remedies alongside physical treatment. The concept of karma-ja-vyādhi (karma-born disease) is a distinct category in Āyurvedic pathology.

## Mathematics

The mathematical principle of karma is the law of conservation: every action has an equal and opposite reaction. Vedic mathematics (Gaṇita) treats karma as the principle of balance — equations must balance, debts must be settled. The concept of ṛṇa (debt) in Vedic mathematics mirrors the karmic debt concept.

## Astronomy

Karma in Jyotiṣa (Vedic astrology): the birth chart (janma-kuṇḍali) is considered a map of prārabdha karma. Planetary positions at birth reflect accumulated karma. The concept of daśā (planetary period) describes the timing of karmic fruition. Graha (planets) are considered agents of karma delivery.

## Metallurgy

In Viśvakarmā tradition: the karma of the craftsman (śilpin) determines the quality of the work. The concept of karma-yoga in craft: the craftsman who works without attachment to results produces the finest work. The dharma of metals (their inherent properties) must be respected — working against a metal's karma produces inferior results.

## Ritual

Karma-kāṇḍa (ritual section of the Vedas) is the primary domain of Mīmāṃsā. The sixteen saṃskāras are karmic rituals that shape the individual's karmic trajectory. Yajña (sacrifice) is the highest karmic act — it purifies accumulated karma and generates positive karma. Prāyaścitta (expiation) rituals neutralize specific karmic debts.

## Symbolism

The wheel (cakra) symbolizes karma's cyclical nature. The scales represent karmic balance. The seed (bīja) represents karma's potential — every action is a seed that will bear fruit. The mirror represents karma's reflective nature — what you do returns to you. The knot (granthi) represents karmic bondage.

## Related Deities

- Yama (Dharmarāja — lord of karmic accounting and death)
- Citragupta (Yama's scribe who records all karma)
- Śani (Saturn — the planet of karmic lessons and consequences)
- Brahmā (the creator who sets karma in motion)
- Viṣṇu (the preserver who maintains karmic order)

## Related Lokas

- Naraka (hell realms — destination of negative karma)
- Svarga (heaven realms — destination of positive karma)
- Pitṛloka (realm of ancestors — intermediate karmic state)
- Bhūloka (earth — the primary field of karmic action)

## Related Koshas

- Kāraṇa Śarīra (causal body) — the storehouse of accumulated karma (sañcita karma)
- Sūkṣma Śarīra (subtle body) — the vehicle through which karma is experienced
- Manomaya Kosha (mind sheath) — where karmic intentions originate

## Related Chakras

- Maṇipūra (solar plexus chakra) — seat of will, action, and karmic agency
- Mūlādhāra (root chakra) — seat of prārabdha karma and survival instincts
- Svādhiṣṭhāna (sacral chakra) — seat of karmic desires and creative action

## Related Yantras

- Karma Yantra (used in rituals for karmic purification)
- Śani Yantra (for mitigating difficult karmic periods)

## Related Mantras

- "Karmaṇy evādhikāras te mā phaleṣu kadācana" (Bhagavad Gītā 2.47) — You have the right to action alone, never to its fruits
- Mahāmṛtyuñjaya Mantra (for liberation from karmic death-cycle)
- Śani Mantra: "Om śam śanaiścarāya namaḥ" (for karmic lessons)

## Related Vidyās

- Karma-Yoga Vidyā (science of action without attachment)
- Jyotiṣa Vidyā (science of karmic timing)
- Prāyaścitta Vidyā (science of karmic expiation)

## Related Śāstras

- Bhagavad Gītā (Chapters 3, 4, 5 — Karma Yoga)
- Mīmāṃsā Sūtras (Jaimini) — ritual karma
- Yoga Sūtras (Patañjali) 2.12-14 — karma-āśaya
- Tattvartha Sūtra (Umāsvāti) — Jain karma doctrine
- Caraka Saṃhitā — karmic disease

## Traditional Interpretations

- Advaita Vedānta (Śaṅkara): Karma is ultimately unreal from the absolute standpoint; jñāna (knowledge) alone destroys karma
- Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja): Karma is real and must be surrendered to Viṣṇu through prapatti (surrender)
- Dvaita (Madhva): Karma is eternally real; liberation requires Viṣṇu's grace to transcend karma
- Mīmāṃsā: Karma (ritual action) is the primary means of achieving all human goals
- Buddhism: Karma is intentional action (cetanā); it is the intention, not the act, that creates karma
- Jainism: Karma is a subtle material substance that binds the soul; liberation requires exhausting all karma through tapas (austerity)

## Historical Evolution

- Ṛgvedic period: Karma primarily means ritual action; cosmic karma (ṛta) governs the universe
- Brāhmaṇa period: Karma as ritual action is elaborated extensively; karma-kāṇḍa develops
- Upaniṣadic period: Karma as ethical-spiritual principle emerges; karma-saṃsāra connection established
- Buddhist period (500 BCE): Karma redefined as intentional action; karma-rebirth doctrine systematized
- Jain period: Karma as material substance — unique and influential formulation
- Epic-Purāṇic period: Karma as cosmic justice mechanism; karma-yoga as path to liberation
- Medieval: Karma integrated into bhakti traditions — karma surrendered to God

## Cross References

- Dharma
- Moksha
- Yoga
- Saṃskāra
- Punarjanma (rebirth)
- Ahaṃkāra (ego — the false doer)
- Vāsanā (latent tendencies)

## Open Research Questions

- Is karma a deterministic or probabilistic system? Can free will operate within karma?
- What is the relationship between Vedic karma (ritual action) and Buddhist karma (intentional action)?
- How does the Jain material karma theory relate to the Vedic subtle-body karma theory?

## Experimental Hypotheses

[EXPERIMENTAL — NOT CANONICAL] Some researchers propose that karma theory anticipates modern concepts of information conservation in physics — that the "information" of every action is preserved in the universe. This remains speculative and is not established in any canonical tradition.

## Canonical Sources

- Bhagavad Gītā 2.47, 3.5, 4.17
- Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.13 (karma-rebirth connection)
- Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10 (karma and rebirth)
- Yoga Sūtras 2.12-14
- Tattvartha Sūtra (Umāsvāti) — Jain karma
- Mīmāṃsā Sūtras (Jaimini)

"Ahimsa-satya-asteya-brahmacharya-aparigraha yamah" — Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the five restraints.

Patanjali states (Yoga Sutras 2.35): "Ahimsa-pratishthayam tat-sannidhau vaira-tyagah" — When one is established in non-violence, all enmity is abandoned in one's presence.

## Dharma Connection

The Mahabharata (Anushasana Parva) states: "Ahimsa paramo dharma" — Non-violence is the highest dharma. The Caraka Samhita (Ayurvedic text) states that the physician's svadharma includes ahimsa (non-harm) as the first ethical principle. Dharma.md cross-references Ahimsa as a related concept.

## Cosmology and Ethics

Ahimsa operates at multiple levels:
- Physical: not harming the body of any being
- Verbal: not speaking words that harm
- Mental: not harboring harmful thoughts

In Jain cosmology, every act of violence (himsa) generates karma that binds the soul. Ahimsa is therefore both an ethical principle and a metaphysical necessity for liberation (moksha).

# Dharma

## Canonical Name

Dharma

## Sanskrit

धर्म

## Transliteration

Dharma

## Śabda

धर्म

## Dhātu

धृ (Dhṛ) — To uphold, sustain, support.

## Vyākaraṇa

Derived from the verbal root धृ (dhṛ) with the suffix -man. Masculine noun, second declension. Pāṇini Ashtadhyayi 3.3.18 governs the suffix formation.

## Nirukta

Yāska's Nirukta: "dharayati iti dharmaḥ" — that which upholds is Dharma. The root dhṛ carries the sense of bearing, sustaining, maintaining cosmic and social order.

## Bīja

ध (Dha) — the seed syllable associated with sustaining force in Tantric traditions.

## Tattva

Ṛta-Dharma Tattva — the principle of cosmic and moral order that sustains all existence. In Sāṃkhya: Dharma is a quality (guṇa) of the Mahat (cosmic intellect). In Vedānta: Dharma is the expression of Ṛta at the human level.

## Śakti

Dharma-Śakti — the preserving and ordering power. Associated with Viṣṇu's sustaining function (sthiti-śakti). In Śākta traditions, Dharma is upheld by the Goddess as Mahāmāyā maintaining cosmic law.

## Literal Meaning

That which is upheld; that which upholds. The sustaining principle.

## Functional Meaning

Dharma is the universal principle governing righteous conduct, cosmic order, social duty, and individual ethics. It operates simultaneously at four levels: Ṛta (cosmic order), Varṇāśrama-dharma (social order), Svadharma (individual duty), and Sādhāraṇa-dharma (universal ethics applicable to all beings).

## Marathi Summary

धर्म म्हणजे योग्य आचरण, सामाजिक कर्तव्य, वैश्विक व्यवस्था आणि सर्वांसाठी लागू होणारी नैतिकता टिकवून ठेवणारे तत्त्व.

## Ontology

In Vaiśeṣika: Dharma is a padārtha (category of reality) — the cause of abhyudaya (worldly prosperity) and niḥśreyasa (liberation). In Mīmāṃsā: Dharma is codanā-lakṣaṇa — that which is enjoined by Vedic injunction. In Advaita Vedānta: Dharma at the vyāvahārika (conventional) level is real and necessary; at the pāramārthika (absolute) level, only Brahman exists.

## Cosmology

Dharma is one of the four Puruṣārthas (aims of human life): Dharma, Artha, Kāma, Mokṣa. In the Purāṇic cosmology, Dharma is personified as a deity, son of Brahmā, husband of ten daughters of Dakṣa. In the four yugas (Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, Kali), Dharma stands on four legs, three, two, and one respectively — indicating progressive decline of cosmic order.

## Psychology

In Yoga psychology (Patañjali): Dharma-megha-samādhi is the highest samādhi, the "cloud of virtue" that rains liberation. Dharma as psychological principle governs the sattva-rajas-tamas balance in the individual. Right action (dharmic action) produces psychological clarity (citta-prasāda).

## Governance

Rājadharma (royal duty) is elaborated in Manusmṛti, Arthaśāstra, Mahābhārata Śāntiparva. The king's primary duty is dharma-rakṣaṇa (protection of dharma). Kauṭilya's Arthaśāstra treats dharma as the foundation of statecraft. Aśoka's dhamma edicts represent the historical application of dharmic governance.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: Dharma is the foundation of Āyurvedic ethics. The physician's svadharma includes ahiṃsā (non-harm), satya (truth), and service. Caraka Saṃhitā Sūtrasthāna 1.15 states that the physician who follows dharma achieves both worldly success and liberation.

## Mathematics

Dharma as cosmic order underlies the mathematical precision of Vedic ritual geometry (Śulbasūtras). The Pythagorean theorem appears in Baudhāyana Śulbasūtra as a dharmic requirement for altar construction. Mathematical truth (satya) is considered a form of dharma.

## Astronomy

Ṛta (cosmic order, precursor to dharma) governs the movements of celestial bodies. Vedic astronomy (Jyotiṣa) treats planetary motion as dharmic — planets follow their ordained paths. The concept of ṛtu (season) derives from ṛta, linking dharma to astronomical cycles.

## Metallurgy

In Viśvakarmā tradition: the dharma of metals is their inherent nature and proper use. Gold (suvarṇa) has the dharma of purity; iron (ayasa) has the dharma of strength. Proper metallurgical practice follows the dharma of each material.

## Ritual

Yajña (sacrifice) is the primary ritual expression of dharma. The Mīmāṃsā school holds that Vedic ritual injunctions (vidhi) define dharma. Dharma-śāstra prescribes the sixteen saṃskāras (life-cycle rituals) as the ritual framework of dharmic life. Sandhyāvandana (daily worship) is the minimal dharmic ritual obligation.

## Symbolism

Dharma is symbolized by the wheel (dharmacakra) — the Buddha's first teaching is the "turning of the wheel of dharma." The scales of justice represent dharma's balancing function. The lotus represents dharma's purity amid worldly existence. The cow (go) is the living symbol of dharma in Vedic tradition.

## Traditional Interpretations

- Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja): Dharma is bhakti-yoga — devotional service to Viṣṇu is the highest dharma
- Dvaita (Madhva): Dharma is the eternal will of Viṣṇu; individual dharma is participation in divine order
- Mīmāṃsā (Jaimini): Dharma is exclusively Vedic injunction; no dharma exists outside Veda
- Buddhism: Dharma is the teaching of the Buddha and the nature of reality (dhamma)
- Jainism: Dharma is the medium of motion (one of the six dravyas); also righteous conduct (dharma)

## Historical Evolution

- Ṛgvedic period: Ṛta (cosmic order) is the precursor; dharma appears rarely
- Atharvaveda: Dharma begins to acquire social and ethical dimensions
- Upaniṣadic period: Dharma becomes internalized as ethical-spiritual principle
- Epic period (Mahābhārata): Dharma becomes the central problematic — the Gītā's entire teaching is dharmic
- Dharmaśāstra period (200 BCE–1200 CE): Systematic codification of dharma in law texts
- Colonial period: Dharma reinterpreted through encounter with Western legal concepts
- Modern: Dharma as "religion" (mistranslation) vs. dharma as cosmic-ethical principle (ongoing debate)

# Karma

## Canonical Name

Karma

## Sanskrit

कर्म

## Transliteration

Karma

## Śabda

कर्म

## Dhātu

कृ (Kṛ) — To do, perform, act, make.

## Vyākaraṇa

Derived from the verbal root कृ (kṛ) with the suffix -man (neuter noun). Pāṇini Ashtadhyayi 3.3.18. Karma is a neuter noun meaning "action" or "deed." In grammar, karma also denotes the object of a verb (karman = object/patient).

## Nirukta

Yāska: "kriyate anena iti karma" — that by which action is performed. The root kṛ encompasses all forms of doing, making, and performing.

## Bīja

क (Ka) — the seed syllable of action and creation in Tantric traditions. Associated with Brahmā (the creator) whose bīja is also Ka.

## Tattva

Karma-Tattva — the principle of causation through action. In Sāṃkhya: karma is the activity of the three guṇas (sattva, rajas, tamas). In Vaiśeṣika: karma is one of the seven padārthas (categories), defined as motion. In Vedānta: karma is the mechanism of saṃsāra (cycle of rebirth).

## Śakti

Kriyā-Śakti — the power of action. One of the three fundamental śaktis (icchā-jñāna-kriyā). Karma operates through kriyā-śakti as the dynamic force of manifestation.

## Literal Meaning

Action; deed; work; ritual act.

## Functional Meaning

Karma is the universal principle that every action generates corresponding consequences. It operates across three dimensions: Sañcita karma (accumulated past actions), Prārabdha karma (karma currently bearing fruit), and Āgāmi/Kriyamāṇa karma (karma being created now). The law of karma is not punishment but the natural law of cause and effect operating through consciousness.

## Ontology

In Mīmāṃsā: karma (ritual action) is the primary means of achieving dharmic results; the apūrva (unseen potency) of ritual karma persists until it bears fruit. In Advaita Vedānta: karma operates only at the vyāvahārika level; from the absolute standpoint, there is no doer, hence no karma. In Viśiṣṭādvaita: karma is real and must be exhausted through bhakti and surrender to Viṣṇu. In Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika: karma is one of seven categories of reality, defined as motion (pariṇāma).

## Cosmology

Karma drives the cycle of saṃsāra across all fourteen lokas. The Purāṇas describe karma as the mechanism by which souls transmigrate through different realms. In Jain cosmology, karma is a subtle material substance (karma-pudgala) that adheres to the soul (jīva) and determines its condition. The Bhāgavata Purāṇa describes karma as the force that maintains the cosmic order of creation, preservation, and dissolution.

## Psychology

In Yoga psychology: karma creates saṃskāras (mental impressions) and vāsanās (latent tendencies) that condition future experience. Patañjali's Yoga Sūtras 2.12-14 describe the karma-āśaya (karma-store) as the root of birth, lifespan, and experience. Karma operates through the kāraṇa-śarīra (causal body). Karma yoga (the yoga of action) transforms karma from bondage to liberation by eliminating the sense of doership (ahaṃkāra).

## Governance

Karma as social principle: the concept of karma-phala (fruit of action) underlies Indian jurisprudence. Kauṭilya's Arthaśāstra recognizes that rulers accumulate karma through their governance. The concept of rāja-dharma (royal duty) is the karmic responsibility of the king. Historical Indian governance was explicitly framed in karmic terms — Aśoka's dhamma edicts reflect karmic accountability.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: karma is one of the causes of disease (prājñāparādha — crime against wisdom is a karmic cause). Caraka Saṃhitā identifies karma as a factor in the etiology of disease. Karmic diseases (ādhidaivika) require spiritual remedies alongside physical treatment. The concept of karma-ja-vyādhi (karma-born disease) is a distinct category in Āyurvedic pathology.

## Mathematics

The mathematical principle of karma is the law of conservation: every action has an equal and opposite reaction. Vedic mathematics (Gaṇita) treats karma as the principle of balance — equations must balance, debts must be settled. The concept of ṛṇa (debt) in Vedic mathematics mirrors the karmic debt concept.

## Astronomy

Karma in Jyotiṣa (Vedic astrology): the birth chart (janma-kuṇḍali) is considered a map of prārabdha karma. Planetary positions at birth reflect accumulated karma. The concept of daśā (planetary period) describes the timing of karmic fruition. Graha (planets) are considered agents of karma delivery.

## Metallurgy

In Viśvakarmā tradition: the karma of the craftsman (śilpin) determines the quality of the work. The concept of karma-yoga in craft: the craftsman who works without attachment to results produces the finest work. The dharma of metals (their inherent properties) must be respected — working against a metal's karma produces inferior results.

## Ritual

Karma-kāṇḍa (ritual section of the Vedas) is the primary domain of Mīmāṃsā. The sixteen saṃskāras are karmic rituals that shape the individual's karmic trajectory. Yajña (sacrifice) is the highest karmic act — it purifies accumulated karma and generates positive karma. Prāyaścitta (expiation) rituals neutralize specific karmic debts.

## Symbolism

The wheel (cakra) symbolizes karma's cyclical nature. The scales represent karmic balance. The seed (bīja) represents karma's potential — every action is a seed that will bear fruit. The mirror represents karma's reflective nature — what you do returns to you. The knot (granthi) represents karmic bondage.
